newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New port litmus test for South African investment.
newsitem.headline: New port litmus test for South African investment.

text.p: On a windswept stretch of beach north of Port Elizabeth plans are afoot for a brand new port, a litmus test for badly needed direct investment in South Africa.

Local officials, briefing journalists this week, said the proposed bulk harbour at Coega and an adjacent Industrial Development Zone could double the area's economy and dent one of the country's highest unemployment rates of 40-50 percent.

But whether the ambitious project sees the light of day depends on government, which will have to stump up some 700 million rand ($160 million) to kick-start the scheme, and the commitment of a handful of risk-taking companies.

Technically, Coega looks viable as a port capable of handling ships of up to 80,000 deadweight tonnes. A feasibility study will be completed next month and port operator Portnet hopes government will then commit to help with basic infrastructure, notably construction of a breakwater.

Kevin Wakeford, chief executive of the Port Elizabeth Chamber of Commerce, says the rationale for Coega is the shift in the South African economy from import substitution to export-driven manufacturing.
"In line with the export orientation of government policy, there is a natural shift of industry to the coast," he said, adding that other ports were becoming congested.

Catalyst for the scheme is a planned 220,000-tonnes-a-year zinc refinery by Gencor Ltd and a neighbouring fertiliser plant proposed by AECI unit Kynoch -- together representing investment of 2.3 billion rand.
But Coega hopes many other concerns will set up shop on the 10,000 hectare industrial area behind the harbour.

South Africa needs more fixed investment if government is to meet its goal of doubling annual economic growth to six percent by 2000 -- and the Eastern Cape where Coega is situated needs it more than most. The region has 16 percent of the country's population but accounts for only 7.5 percent of GDP.

"The hope must be that this will be mark a fundamental beginning of new, virtuous investment cycle in that part of the world," said Ben van Rensburg, director of economic policy at the South African Chamber of Business.

However, the project remains a gamble. Coega's backers say the port is equidistant from South Africa's three economic heartlands around Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban -- critics say it is a long way from any of them.
Other companies interested in establishing plants at Coega include Pretoria Portland Cement Ltd, Samancor, Iscor, Afrox and Willard Batteries.
But the real prize will be foreign investment in South African bricks and mortar.

After years of disinvestment, foreign firms are moving back gingerly to South Africa. However, their direct investment -- estimated at around four billion rand in 1996 -- remains small by comparison with the portfolio funds which have flooded in stocks and bonds this year on the back of a recovering rand.
Those short-term funds can flee as fast as they came in. An investment in plant would show real long-term commitment to wealth and job creation in South Africa, analysts say.
